title: The sea-level budget closed in 2005-2015, but altimetry exceeded Argo steric plus GRACE-FO ocean mass by 6-9 mm in 2020.5-2024 in 12 product combinations; salinity and Sentinel-6MF do not explain it
abstract: Question: is the slower GRACE-FO ocean-mass gain after 2018 also in altimetry minus Argo steric sea level? Approach: we made 12 budget combinations from two altimetry GMSL products (CU 2026_rel2, NOAA LSA), two steric products (our TEOS-10 0-2000 dbar computation from the Roemmich-Gilson Argo grid, NCEI 0-2000 m thermosteric) and two mascon solutions (GSFC RL06v2.0, CSR RL06.3), 2005.0-2026.5, with a 0.1 mm/yr deep term and block-bootstrap errors. Results: the budget closed in 2005.0-2016.0 (residual trend -0.13 to +0.15 mm/yr). In 2018.5-2025.1 the residual trend was +0.88 to +1.29 mm/yr. The residual level in 2020.5-2024.0 was 5.6-8.7 mm above its 2005-2015 mean in all 12 combinations; same-length 2005-2015 excursions stayed below 1.9 mm. The gap stayed with thermosteric sea level only (5.6-7.9 mm). Sentinel-6MF minus Jason-3 drifted 0.07 +/- 0.17 mm/yr over 2021-2025, so the reference change did not cause it. Growth started near 2016 and was largest in 2019.5-2021. GRACE mass rates fell (GSFC 2.24 to 1.54 mm/yr, mostly Antarctica and Greenland), but altimetry minus Argo rose (2.29-2.30 to 2.54-2.63 mm/yr) to early 2025. Thus the GRACE-FO mass slowdown is not confirmed. Limitations: we cannot tell if GRACE-FO mass, Argo-era steric (unsampled deep or marginal ocean) or a drift common to Jason-3 and Sentinel-6MF is wrong; a tide-gauge rate-change test (+0.41 +/- 1.06 mm/yr) was inconclusive; periods are short.

citations.reason: Found the post-2018 GRACE-FO ocean-mass slowdown and the 2025-26 GMSL shortfall. We test the mass slowdown with a closed budget and do not confirm it to early 2025.
